title: President pledges to shed 34 SOEs as Treasury surplus nears Rs. 1 t | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 24 October 2026 00:00
-     - 13

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake

The Treasury account now holds a surplus approaching Rs. 1 trillion, compared with a deficit of about Rs. 700 billion in 2022, while a Finance Ministry committee is considering closing or amalgamating 34 State-owned enterprises (SOEs) deemed unnecessary or inefficient, President Anura Kumara Dissanayake said yesterday.

Addressing the 100th Annual Conference of the Government Surveyors’ Association at the Waters Edge Hotel in Battaramulla, President Dissanayake said the Government had been constantly compelled to print money or borrow from the banking system due to a lack of funds, and the turnaround in the Treasury’s position had helped considerably in resolving the rupee crisis.

He said political appointments made in the past had resulted in excessive staffing at lower levels of the public service, creating a substantial financial burden. “Our aim is to build an attractive public service comprising capable and highly qualified professionals,” he said.

The President said revenue collection in 2025 reached 110% of the projected target, the first time in Sri Lanka’s history, noting that no previous Budget had achieved its projected revenue targets. He said the Government expected to achieve a healthy level of revenue in 2026 by meeting the targets set for the Department of Inland Revenue, the Sri Lanka Customs Department and the Department of Excise.

Sri Lanka recorded a current account surplus of $ 1.8 billion in 2025, he said. Since independence, the country had recorded a current account surplus on only about three occasions, each of about $ 300 million.

However, President Dissanayake said the Middle East conflict had exposed Sri Lanka to an unexpected impact. The country spent $ 4 billion on oil imports last year and had already spent $ 4 billion by the end of August this year, meaning the total could exceed $ 6 billion by year-end. Managing pressure on foreign exchange reserves was therefore one of the main challenges, he said.

The Government plans to increase capital expenditure from Rs. 1,330 billion this year to Rs. 2 trillion next year. The President said a large number of major projects had been launched using domestic Treasury funds alone without borrowing in dollars, including the Kurunegala-Galewela, Rambukkana-Galagedara and Kahathuduwa-Ingiriya Expressways. The Government also plans to begin the estimated Rs. 600 billion Kelani Valley railway line electrification project next year using Treasury funds.

He said that even when expenditure is in rupees, dollars are needed to import machinery, steel and other materials, making earning dollars and minimising dollar outflows the principal economic strategies. While the country now has sufficient rupee resources to withstand domestic shocks, the economy is not yet strong enough to withstand external shocks arising from tourism, foreign workers’ remittances and fuel prices, he said.

On public sector pay, the President said the inability to retain professionals had made it difficult to recruit engineers, IT professionals and managers. The 2025 Budget provided for a basic salary increase in three phases in 2025, 2026 and 2027, each costing Rs. 110 billion, adding Rs. 330 billion to the salary bill by 2027 compared with 2024. As no further basic salary increase is planned in the 2028 Budget, greater consideration could be given to allowances at that stage, he said.

On the surveying service, President Dissanayake said the Government was prepared to allocate the necessary funds in the Budget for modern technological equipment if an assessment study identifying the requirements is submitted. He said the Government would also consider a study to amend the service minute, as requirements differ from those of 20 years ago.

A criminal case concerning the alleged importation, sale, and possession of counterfeit products bearing the Oregon mark is continuing before the Magistrates’ Court of Mawanella, following a raid conducted by officers of the Commercial Crime Investigation Unit 2 (CCIU2) of the Criminal Investigation Department (CID).

The operation was carried out pursuant to a search warrant issued by the Mawanella Magistrate on 8 October 2026 in respect of premises now located at Venas Hall, Hemathagama Road, Mawanella. The case, bearing No. B/11827/26, involves Fumax Marketing Ltd., as the accused and Oregon Tool Inc., USA, the owner of the Oregon brand, as the complainant and aggrieved party.  The allegations relate to products suspected of infringing Oregon Tool Inc.’s trademarks and imitating the presentation of its genuine products.

According to the inventory submitted to court, thousands of suspected counterfeit products were seized during the operation and produced before court on 13 October 2026.

When the matter was called on that date, Deshan Hewavithana, Attorney-at-Law, instructed by Sudath Perera Associates, appeared on behalf of Oregon Tool Inc., USA, while Fumax Marketing Ltd., was represented by Krishantha Herath.

The CID informed court that the search warrant had been successfully executed and submitted a further report. The CID also produced the shop manager before court on police bail. The CID further informed court that the owner of the business was abroad and that further investigations concerning him would be conducted upon his return to Sri Lanka.

The Magistrate subsequently granted bail to the manager subject to a surety of Rs. 100,000.

During the proceedings, the defence counsel made an application concerning certain seized items bearing the letters “OBL,” contending that the relevant items belonged to the accused. However, both the CID and the aggrieved party brought to the court’s attention the similarity between the “OBL” lettering printed on the outer packaging of those items and the registered “DBL” trademark. The latter is registered with the National Intellectual Property Office (NIPO) and is associated with the abbreviated name of Deen Brothers Importers Ltd, (DBL).

Following submissions by both parties, the Magistrate directed the parties to file written submissions addressing the disputed seized items before the next hearing. The matter was accordingly fixed for further consideration on 27 October 2026.

Sri Lanka welcomed 119,805 tourists during the first 22 days of October, registering a 5.03% year-on-year (YoY) increase, but cumulative arrivals remained 1.42% below the corresponding period last year as the industry entered its crucial winter season.

The latest figures lifted year-to-date (YTD) arrivals to over 1.81 million, compared with over 1.83 million during the same period in 2025, highlighting the challenge facing the sector in closing the gap before the end of the year and also to maximise tourism earnings from the arrivals secured.

Average daily arrivals increased to 5,446 during the first 22 days of October, from 5,185 in the corresponding period last year with the highest daily footfall at 7,045 visitors on 17 October. Arrivals were registered at 35,786 in the first week of October and 35,400 in the second, before rising to 42,739 in the third week. A further 5,880 visitors arrived on 22 October.

India remained Sri Lanka’s largest source market, accounting for 45,530 visitors, or 38% of arrivals during the period. The UK followed with 8,678 visitors (7%), closely followed by China with 8,430 (7%). Australia contributed 6,064 visitors (5%), while Germany accounted for 5,642 (5%).

Cumulative figures continued to underline India’s dominance, with 482,944 arrivals, representing 27% of the total arrivals. The UK ranked second with 169,405 visitors (9%), followed by China with 120,980 (7%), Germany with 102,920 (6%) and Australia with 93,053 (5%).

The October improvement comes as the tourism industry approaches its traditionally strong winter travel period, which will be critical in determining whether Sri Lanka can regain momentum and move closer to its annual arrival target.

However, the sector remains some distance from its pre-crisis performance. Sri Lanka recorded around 1.88 million tourist arrivals by the end of October 2018, against which the country would need approximately another 80,000 visitors to reach that benchmark based on the cumulative figure reported for 22 October 2026.

The Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority (SLTDA) revised its full-year arrival projections in September amid the continuing impact of the Middle East conflict, higher energy costs and uncertainty surrounding international travel.

title: Welfare net fails to track household shocks: IPS | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 24 October 2026 00:00
-     - 5

IPS Research Fellow Dr. Ganga Tilakaratna – Pic by Ruwan Walpola

Sri Lanka’s social protection system reaches households regardless of how exposed they are to shocks, the Institute of Policy Studies (IPS) said. This leaves many of the poorest and most shock-hit households without support.

IPS Research Fellow Dr. Ganga Tilakaratna presented the findings at a roundtable yesterday on the IPS flagship report, Sri Lanka State of the Economy 2026. She drew on two chapters, one on shock-responsive social protection and one on a health-centred silver economy (economic activity built around the needs and capacities of an ageing population). She said both were relevant to building the resilience needed for durable growth.

Dr. Tilakaratna said the COVID-19 pandemic, the 2022 economic crisis and repeated climate disasters had exposed many households to multiple, overlapping shocks.

To measure this, the IPS built a household shock exposure index from an integrated household survey of about 6,850 households. The index captures cumulative exposure to 13 types of shock, weighted by severity. It classifies households as facing low, medium or high exposure. About 11.4% of households, or one in nine, fell into the high exposure group, and more than half faced moderate exposure.

Close to 30% of households received Aswesuma welfare benefits, and about 50% received benefits from at least one social protection program. In the estate sector, which has historically had the highest poverty, 54% of households received Aswesuma benefits. Dr. Tilakaratna described this as a notable improvement on the coverage of the previous Samurdhi program.

However, coverage did not rise with shock exposure. At national level, Aswesuma coverage was broadly the same across all three exposure groups. The rural sector followed the national pattern, and the urban sector showed no clear pattern. In the estate sector, coverage was lower among high-exposure households than among low-exposure ones, although still above rural and urban levels. “Overall, we don’t find any consistent relationship between household shock exposure and coverage,” Dr. Tilakaratna said. This applied both to Aswesuma and to the wider system.

By income, coverage was broadly pro-poor, with poorer households more likely to receive support. Still, only 62.5% of households in the bottom expenditure quintile received social protection, leaving over a third uncovered. Among bottom-quintile households facing high shock exposure, coverage fell to 55%. This was below the rate for their less-exposed peers in the same quintile, leaving about 45% without support.

Dr. Tilakaratna said this showed the need to widen coverage and strengthen the system’s capacity to respond to shocks, so that vulnerable households do not fall into poverty or lose income. She suggested exploring whether Aswesuma eligibility could better reflect household exposure to shocks, including climate shocks.

The IPS set out five priorities. The first is to bring all social protection programs into the Integrated Welfare Management System, whose social registry covers about 3.4 million households. That registry should expand to cover vulnerable households currently outside the system. The second is to link social protection with disaster management and climate information, to identify vulnerable households in disaster-prone areas. The third is to create mechanisms for rapid expansion during crises, such as predefined expansion protocols and financing arrangements. The fourth is to strengthen digital payments for timely delivery. The fifth is to invest more in labour market and productive inclusion programs, which build long-term resilience.

On ageing, Dr. Tilakaratna said rapid population ageing poses challenges for social protection and healthcare. It also creates an opportunity to develop a silver economy that supports healthy and productive ageing. The IPS assessed the health system across six building blocks and found gaps, including [a shortage of age-disaggregated health information], supply disruptions and no mechanism for financing long-term care.

The IPS proposed three responses. The first is stronger primary healthcare, with better integration of chronic disease and elderly care and better referral pathways. The second is wider use of telemedicine, electronic health records and remote monitoring, alongside efforts to close digital literacy gaps among vulnerable groups. The third is financial protection for older people, by cutting out-of-pocket spending through better access to essential medicines and targeted subsidies.

title: Treasury hails Sri Lanka Customs’ contributions to recovery, development | Daily FT

Saturday, 24 October 2026 00:00

Treasury Secretary 

Dr. Harshana Suriyapperuma

Sri Lanka Customs Director General 

Vimal Liyanagama

Treasury Secretary Dr. Harshana Suriyapperuma has hailed Sri Lanka Customs’ (SLC) contributions to the country’s recovery and development, saying revenue collected by the department enabled the Government to allocate Rs. 500 billion to respond to the Ditwah disaster and to provide relief on fuel prices driven up by the war in the Middle East.

He made the remarks at a ceremony held on Thursday at the Customs Department to felicitate officers after SLC surpassed its full-year revenue target for 2026 with more than two months of the year remaining.

Dr. Suriyapperuma said Customs revenue is used for the welfare of the people, funding infrastructure, education, healthcare, investment for the country’s future needs and emergency relief.

He said international institutions act to raise Sri Lanka’s credit ratings taking into account the stability of the economy, and the efficient performance of the Government’s revenue-collecting institutions is an important factor in this.

SLC collected Rs. 2,208 billion on 13 October, exceeding its 2026 target of Rs. 2,207 billion, and total collections had risen to Rs. 2.29 trillion as at 21 October, the Finance Ministry said yesterday. The department exceeded its revenue target in every month of 2026.

In 2025, SLC met its annual target on 11 November. This year it achieved a higher target 29 days earlier.

Dr. Suriyapperuma stressed the importance of transforming SLC into an efficient institution operating to international standards. He said it was very important to make customs operations more efficient through modern technology to further improve revenue collection, and to curb fraud by sharing information collected by Customs with other relevant sectors.

He said that, despite obstacles, SLC had implemented its paperless customs declaration programme.

Dr. Suriyapperuma said SLC has the capacity to raise revenue further, and that further developing the legal system and governance structure could improve public, business and trade association attitudes towards the department.

Sri Lanka Customs Director General Vimal Liyanagama said achieving the target was the result of the work of a dedicated, professionally skilled team of officers.

The Government plans to establish 18 new industrial zones as it seeks to attract investment, expand manufacturing capacity and position itself as a regional hub for trade, technology and industry, Industry and Entrepreneurship Development Deputy Minister Chathuranga Abeysinghe said.  

Speaking at the NDTV World Summit 2026 in New Delhi, India, during a discussion on “Sri Lanka’s Economic Reset: Recovery, Resilience and the Road Ahead”, Abeysinghe said the country was shifting from economic stabilisation towards sustainable growth and called on international investors to participate in its next phase of development.

Abeysinghe said Sri Lanka had the potential to become a regional centre for trade, research and development, technology and skilled talent. He called on the international businesses to move beyond supporting the country’s recovery and become partners in its long-term growth.

“Don’t just support Sri Lanka’s recovery, be part of its growth,” he said.

He also encouraged foreign companies to work with established Sri Lankan enterprises through investments, technology transfers and greater access to international markets.

Identifying opportunities for stronger economic cooperation between Sri Lanka and India, the Deputy Minister highlighted manufacturing, agricultural value addition, logistics, renewable energy, marine industries and technology as sectors with potential for mutually beneficial partnerships.

He said the Government was also working to simplify investment procedures, digitise public services and improve regulatory clarity to create a more investor-friendly business environment.

Abeysinghe stressed that sustained economic reforms, stronger governance, digital transformation and industrial development would be critical to strengthening Sri Lanka’s long-term resilience and competitiveness.

title: Prof. Sarath Kodithuwakku: Legacy beyond lecture hall | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 24 October 2026 00:00
-     - 10

Prof. Sarath S. Kodithuwakku

A memento being presented to Prof. Sivananthan of Sivananthan Laboratories Inc., USA in appreciation of its generous sponsorship to forge and sustain collaborations with the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (UIUC)

A memento being presented to former University of Illinois System Vice-Chancellor and President Prof. Robert Easter for the same purpose

As Prof. Sarath S. Kodithuwakku retires from the University of Peradeniya on 24 October, 2026, his distinguished career reflects a lasting contribution to academic innovation, institution building and the transformation of management and agricultural education in Sri Lanka.

The contribution of an academic is often measured through research publications, qualifications, administrative positions and years of service. Yet the true significance of an academic career is sometimes better reflected in the institutions established, the opportunities created and the generations of students whose lives have been influenced along the way.

Prof. Kodithuwakku represents this broader dimension of academic achievement.

Over more than three decades, his contributions have extended across agricultural education, business management, entrepreneurship, postgraduate studies, research and university administration. A defining characteristic of his career has been his willingness to challenge conventional academic boundaries and introduce initiatives that connect university education with the evolving needs of industry and society.

Redefining agricultural higher education

One of Prof. Kodithuwakku’s most significant contributions has been his role in broadening the traditional scope of agricultural education.

At a time when agricultural studies were predominantly associated with production and the sciences, he recognised the growing importance of integrating business management, marketing and entrepreneurship into agricultural education.

This thinking contributed to the evolution of the Department of Agricultural Economics into the Department of Agricultural Economics and Business Management at the University of Peradeniya, reflecting a more commercially oriented and multidisciplinary approach.

His contribution to curriculum development was equally important. As Chairman of the Curriculum Committee and subsequently as Dean of the Faculty of Agriculture, he played a leading role in initiating the revision of the BSc Honours in Agricultural Technology and Management degree program, which included the introduction of a major-minor structure that offered students greater academic flexibility.

He also pioneered an innovative approach to promoting agricultural higher education, introducing structured branding and marketing communication to reposition the degree and broaden public understanding of its professional opportunities.

These initiatives reflected his conviction that universities must continuously evolve to remain relevant to changing economic and professional realities.

Bringing management education beyond Colombo

Among his most enduring institutional achievements was the establishment of the Master of Business Administration (MBA) program at the Postgraduate Institute of Agriculture (PGIA), University of Peradeniya, in 1998.

It was the first MBA program offered outside Colombo and the third established by a Sri Lankan state university.

At a time when postgraduate management education was largely concentrated in the capital, this initiative marked an important step towards widening access to advanced management education.

As Founder Coordinator, Prof. Kodithuwakku played a central role in establishing and developing the program. He subsequently contributed to establishing the Board of Study in Business Administration and introduced the Doctor of Business Administration (DBA) program at PGIA in 2005, further extending the Institute’s contribution to postgraduate management education.

The MBA program has since provided opportunities for professionals, managers and entrepreneurs to advance their knowledge, while strengthening the connection between academic learning and organisational practice.

Its continuing relevance is an example of institution building whose influence extends far beyond the tenure of its founder.

Turning entrepreneurship into experience

Prof. Kodithuwakku’s approach to teaching was shaped by a fundamental belief: entrepreneurship cannot be adequately understood through theory alone.

This philosophy led to the introduction of Business Creation and Management, an undergraduate course that encouraged students to establish and operate real business ventures.

The initiative went beyond conventional classroom instruction, allowing students to experience the practical challenges of entrepreneurship, financial management and commercial decision-making.

Profits generated through these ventures were reinvested in student development, supporting participation in international academic conferences and sporting events. The student fund also enabled the establishment of four gold medals recognising excellence in Business Management and Agricultural Economics.

A similar philosophy underpinned The Kiosk, a student-managed restaurant developed with the support of the Faculty and its alumni. Beyond generating income for students, it served as a practical learning environment for developing entrepreneurial, business and managerial capabilities.

Together, these initiatives demonstrated how academic innovation could simultaneously strengthen education, entrepreneurship and student welfare.

A commitment to students that began early

An equally meaningful contribution began in 1990 when Prof. Kodithuwakku, then an undergraduate, joined his batchmates in establishing the Needy Students Scholarship Fund at the Faculty of Agriculture.

Conceived as a collective effort to assist financially disadvantaged students, the initiative gradually developed into an enduring tradition of student-supported fundraising.

Successive undergraduate batches sustained the 

program, which eventually became associated with the annual Indeewaree Musical Show.

The fund has since grown to approximately Rs. 15 million and continues to support students facing financial difficulties.

What makes this initiative particularly noteworthy is that it originated long before Prof. Kodithuwakku assumed any formal academic leadership position. It reflected an early understanding that higher education carries responsibilities extending beyond individual academic advancement.

Connecting universities with the wider economy

Prof. Kodithuwakku also played an important role in strengthening the relationship between university research and practical economic development.

His involvement with the Agribusiness Centre of the University of Peradeniya, dating back to its establishment in 1997, contributed to the development of an institutional platform connecting academic expertise with agricultural enterprises, industry and rural communities.

His research and consultancy work encompassed agricultural marketing, entrepreneurship, food security, value-chain development and smallholder livelihoods, involving collaborations with national and international development and research organisations.

His international academic experience included serving as an Assistant Professor at Sultan Qaboos University in Oman from 2011 to 2016, further enriching his contribution to teaching, research and institutional development.

More recently, he provided strategic leadership in initiating an international research collaboration involving Prof. Sivananthan of Sivananthan Laboratories Inc., USA, the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (UIUC), the Faculty of Agriculture of the University of Peradeniya and Sri Lanka’s Department of Agriculture. The collaboration focuses on soybean varietal trials to strengthen domestic soybean production, while also fostering academic collaboration between the two universities to enhance agricultural education and research.

These engagements demonstrated his consistent interest in ensuring that universities contribute meaningfully to national development.

Leadership through challenging times

Prof. Kodithuwakku served as Dean of the Faculty of Agriculture from November 2021 to November 2024, during one of the most difficult periods experienced by Sri Lankan universities.

The aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic and the country’s economic crisis created unprecedented institutional and operational challenges.

Despite these pressures, his tenure saw continued attention to curriculum reform, academic development, institutional partnerships and student welfare.

His leadership experience also included four terms as Head of the Department of Agricultural Economics and Business Management and several appointments as Acting Vice-Chancellor of the University of Peradeniya.

Beyond academia, he contributed extensively to professional management education, including leadership of the Institute of Management of Sri Lanka and longstanding involvement with the Sri Lanka Institute of Marketing.

His role in advancing professional management education and recognition initiatives further strengthened the relationship between academia and Sri Lanka’s business community.

A legacy that will endure

Across his academic career, Prof. Kodithuwakku has supervised approximately 200 undergraduate dissertations and 100 MBA dissertations, alongside doctoral research mentorship, scholarly publications and numerous institutional responsibilities.

Yet perhaps his most significant contribution cannot be adequately expressed through these conventional measures.

The MBA program he established continues to educate professionals. The curriculum reforms he championed have broadened the possibilities available to agricultural graduates. His entrepreneurship initiatives have helped translate academic knowledge into practical experience, while the scholarship fund he helped establish as an undergraduate continues to support new generations of students.

These contributions share an important characteristic: their value extends beyond the individual who initiated them.

As Prof. Kodithuwakku concludes his distinguished service at the University of Peradeniya, his career offers a compelling reminder that academic leadership is ultimately about more than personal accomplishment. It is about building institutions, challenging established thinking and creating opportunities that endure.

While his formal academic career comes to a close, the programs, institutions and generations of students shaped by his contribution ensure that his influence will continue well beyond the lecture halls of Peradeniya.

title: How did Sri Lanka get to war?  ‘Teardrop Nation’ traces road to 2009 | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 24 October 2026 00:00
-     - 11

Teardrop Nation Project Director Sarah Kabir addresses the audience at the premiere in Colombo

Invitees at the premiere of Teardrop Nation in Colombo

Understanding our past is essential to building positive and lasting peace in Sri Lanka. We created Teardrop Nation to make this history more accessible, especially to younger people, and to encourage them to engage with it thoughtfully and critically - Teardrop Nation Project Director Sarah Kabir

By Tania de Silva

Sri Lanka’s post-independence history is marked by political upheaval, discrimination, ethnic tensions, rebellion, violence and war. Yet for generations of young Sri Lankans, much of this history remains fragmented, contested or absent from formal education.

A new four-part documentary series, Teardrop Nation, seeks to address that gap by bringing the country’s political and conflict history to a wider public audience.

The series was formally launched at Scope Cinemas Multiplex at Colombo City Centre on 8 October, with Minister Bimal Rathnayake attending as Chief Guest. 

Developed over six years by Project 72, with Sarah Kabir serving as Project Director, Teardrop Nation combines historical accounts, archival material, expert perspectives and lived experiences to examine the events and decisions that shaped Sri Lanka from the period leading up to independence through the end of the civil war in 2009.

“Understanding our past is essential to building positive and lasting peace in Sri Lanka,” Kabir said. “We created Teardrop Nation to make this history more accessible, especially to younger people, and to encourage them to engage with it thoughtfully and critically.”

Understanding how conflict began

The idea for the documentary grew out of Kabir’s decade of work in reconciliation.

She said that while working in the field, she repeatedly encountered the need to understand the historical roots of Sri Lanka’s conflict. Questions about why the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) emerged, for example, were often difficult to explore without first examining the political and social developments that preceded it.

For Kabir, this highlighted a significant gap.

“There was this lack of understanding of what went wrong,” she said. “Questions such as why the LTTE came to being were rarely asked.”

The team conducted 33 interviews, each averaging around two hours, while consulting more than 40 academics and experts. Five academic consultants were involved throughout the project, providing feedback on scripts and edits and helping the team navigate the complexity of the subject.

The research process also involved extensive archival work, historical journals and books, and conversations with people representing different perspectives.

“It would definitely be the research component that took a lot longer than expected because there was a lot more than I even knew,” Kabir said.

Four episodes, one history

Teardrop Nation unfolds chronologically across four episodes: The Seeds We Sow, The Trigger, Battle for Peace and War in Paradise.

The first episode establishes the foundations of the conflict and begins with Sri Lanka’s transition from colonial rule to independence. At the centre of the episode is a fundamental question: Who are we, and what does it mean to be Sri Lankan? It examines class and caste divisions, economic disparities, constitutional changes and discriminatory policies, while tracing how successive political decisions contributed to growing divisions within society. 

The episode examines developments including the first anti-Tamil pogrom, the Citizenship Act, the Sinhala Only Act and subsequent amendments, the introduction of a new constitution, the Vaddukodai Resolution and economic policies that contributed to growing youth discontent. It also explores the emergence of revolutionary movements in both the North and South, showing how developments taking place in different parts of the country would eventually contribute to widespread violence.

The second episode moves into the period when political and social tensions intensified and eventually developed into armed conflict. It examines the factors surrounding the emergence of the First Eelam War and the consequences of major events such as the burning of the Jaffna Library and Black July. The documentary also seeks to complicate simplified narratives surrounding Tamil political resistance. According to Project 72, the LTTE was not the only group opposing Government policies in the North. Several organisations emerged with different approaches, including groups that did not initially pursue armed struggle. The episode subsequently traces how the LTTE consolidated power and eliminated rival groups.

At the same time, the documentary examines constitutional and economic reforms, increasing authoritarianism and growing unrest in the South, including dissatisfaction among revolutionary movements there.

The result is a picture of a country becoming increasingly polarised, with developments in the North and South unfolding alongside one another.

The third episode examines a period defined by the constant push and pull between war and attempts at peace. It follows efforts by the Government of Sri Lanka and the LTTE to reach political settlements, as well as attempts to secure international involvement in resolving the country’s crises. The Indo-Lanka Accord and its consequences for communities in both the North and South receive significant attention The episode also examines one of the bloodiest periods in Sri Lanka’s post-independence history, including disappearances, intimidation, human rights violations and the assassinations of prominent local and international leaders.

Two major conflicts unfold simultaneously: the confrontation between the JVP and the State in the South and the conflict between the LTTE and the Indian Peace Keeping Force in the North. The episode also gives attention to the experiences of the Muslim community, an aspect of the conflict that Kabir described as often under-explored. It closes in 1999, with a presidential candidate attacked by a suicide bomber, setting the stage for the final episode.

The final episode examines the later stages of the conflict and the human cost of the third and fourth Eelam wars. It follows further attempts at negotiations and ceasefires before renewed warfare, examining not only the confrontation between the LTTE and the Government of Sri Lanka but also internal fractures within these groups. At the heart of the episode is a question that remains deeply contested in Sri Lankan society: Did anyone really win? The conclusion of the war brought an end to large-scale armed conflict, but the documentary places that military ending alongside the immense loss of life, unresolved questions, unacknowledged histories and continuing wounds left by decades of violence. The final episode ultimately brings the audience back to the present and asks how Sri Lanka arrived at where it is today and what it means to share a history shaped by conflict.

A history that is not simply black and white

One of the central principles behind Teardrop Nation is the recognition that history cannot always be reduced to a single narrative.

Kabir said the series deliberately attempts to present different perspectives rather than tell audiences what they should believe. “What I hope to achieve through this is for people to understand that sometimes it's not only your narrative that is the truth,” she said. “There are different versions. There are different beliefs that people hold on to.”

The distinction between fact and interpretation was particularly important to the research process.

Kabir gave the Citizenship Act as an example. The fact that approximately 700,000 people were disenfranchised can be established historically. The motivations behind the decision, however, are more difficult to determine with certainty and can involve interpretation and competing explanations.

Making difficult history accessible to young people

Kabir said the decision to use documentary film rather than a book was partly driven by the need to make the subject more accessible to younger audiences. The series uses clearer language, visual storytelling and creative documentary techniques to make complex historical material more engaging without deliberately simplifying the subject matter. The team also conducted focus groups with younger audiences before completing the series. Rather than limiting the groups to history students, participants came from different professional and academic backgrounds, including marketing and accounting.

The response, Kabir said, was encouraging.

“I was also of the understanding that, okay, will I be able to retain the attention of the younger audience who are used to this TikTok and all of that?” she said.

However, participants remained engaged with the episodes, partly because much of the history was unfamiliar to them.

The project also plans to expand its engagement with young people through schools and universities, including screenings and discussions. Engagement with government schools requires the relevant approvals, while work with private, semi-private and international schools and universities is being pursued.

When history begins to repeat itself

For Kabir, studying the past also revealed patterns that remain relevant to contemporary Sri Lanka. One example was the emergence of anti-Muslim sentiment and violence in more recent years. She said some of the rhetoric and policies directed towards the Muslim community reminded her of earlier patterns of discrimination experienced by Tamils. The documentary therefore does not present discrimination as an isolated event. Instead, it examines how repeated political and social exclusion can gradually deepen divisions. “The war didn't happen overnight,” Kabir said. “It took 30 years of discrimination.” She pointed to the cumulative effects of policies and decisions involving language, citizenship, land and education. “When you start doing these things, it doesn't happen overnight. But as you keep doing and more and more piles on, you create a very polarised community,” she said.

The point is not to equate different periods or communities, but to recognise the potential consequences of policies that marginalise sections of society.

If young people understand how seemingly isolated decisions can contribute to long-term social divisions, Kabir believes they may be better equipped to recognise and challenge similar patterns in the future.

That is at the heart of the project's focus on non-recurrence.

The challenge of preserving Sri Lanka’s own archives

Creating a historical documentary about Sri Lanka also meant confronting another problem: the condition and accessibility of the country’s archives. Kabir described archival research as one of the project's most difficult aspects. She said national archival holdings and audiovisual material are often poorly stored and urgently require restoration and digitisation.

Some television archives, she noted, remain stored on outdated formats for which functioning playback equipment is increasingly difficult to find. For a project attempting to preserve historical memory, the situation presents a contradiction: material that could help future generations understand the country's history exists, but may be physically deteriorating or difficult to access.

Working with institutions also involved lengthy approval processes. Kabir recalled one instance where it took almost a year to obtain archival material after it had already been identified and approved. The problem, she said, highlights the broader need to preserve and digitise Sri Lanka's historical record before it is lost.

Six years of persistence

Kabir acknowledged that the project could at times be overwhelming, particularly while balancing other responsibilities and working through periods of national crisis.

But she said persistence kept the project moving.

“I just don't give up,” she said. “No matter whatever the challenge, we just pushed through or figured a way through around it.”

The final episode proved particularly challenging.

Unlike the earlier periods examined in the series, the end of the war remains relatively recent and highly contested. Many Sri Lankans have personal memories and strongly held views about the events surrounding the final stages of the conflict.

Kabir said the fourth episode therefore went through numerous edits and required additional support from outside the core team.

“It is the episode we're almost traumatised by,” she said.

But she also stressed that its difficulty does not make it a preferred or “better” episode. Rather, its proximity to the present and the sensitivity of the subject matter made it particularly challenging to complete.

Because the four episodes build on one another, Kabir recommends that audiences watch them in chronological order. The four episodes are structured for cinema screening, with two episodes shown together, separated by a short interval.

The series is currently screening at Scope Cinemas at Havelock City and Colombo City Centre

Further screenings and expansion to other cities are expected to be explored.

The ‘comic opera’ in  Colombo’s green heart, “Vihara Mahadevi Park” is a stark pointer to the bizarre and dangerous cultural crossroads at which we have arrived.

 Ven. Kotapola Rahula Thero, a senior prelate of the Kotte Sangha Sabha, was an early participant. He initially described this saffron shindig as a righteous Satyagraha for the “protection of the robe.”

 As I write this missive, it has degenerated into a sacrilegious theatre—a ‘Saffron Circus’ orchestrated by a cabal of politicised priests and defeated opposition factions.

 Choreographed by political manipulators, the often-rowdy lay participants are visibly emboldened by the unconcealed patronage of elements within established ecclesiastical bodies in Colombo. Meanwhile, the Kotte Sri Kalyani Samagri Dharma Maha Sangha Sabha is virtually walking on eggshells.

This ritual was led by infamous figures like Samantha Bhadra (formerly known as Pitiduwe Siridhamma), an absolute apostate wrapped in monastic robes.

 How has Buddhism—specifically Ashokan Buddhism, a philosophy anchored in radical non-violence, mindfulness, and the eradication of the ego—been corrupted into a vehicle for political survival and public cursing? To find answers to this riddle, one must revisit the foundational texts of Sri Lankan political anthropology. The crisis we witness today is not an overnight aberration; it is the logical conclusion of historical processes that have systematically exchanged the ethical core of the Dhamma for the preservation of temporal power.

The ‘Politically Buddhist’ State

The distinguished anthropologist H.L. Seneviratne, in his seminal work The Work of Kings, meticulously demonstrates that the modern ‘theory of the Buddhist State’ in Sri Lanka is a relatively recent ideological construction. Seneviratne argues that this theory was formally articulated and institutionalised by nationalist scholars and monks only after the pivotal General Election of 1956.

Prior to 1956, the Buddhist revivalist movement focused largely on cultural reclamation and education in the face of colonial marginalisation. However, the post-1956 political landscape fundamentally altered the monastic vocation. Ideological entrepreneurs engineered a modern narrative that fused the state, the ethnic identity of the majority, and the preservation of the Sasana into a single, indivisible unit.

The strange alignment of varied actors at Viharamahadevi Park makes complete sense when viewed through the lens of recent electoral shifts, particularly the National People›s Power (NPP) gaining a two-thirds majority under President Anura Kumara Dissanayake. Faced with stark structural irrelevance and impending legal accountability for past follies, defeated opposition groups have resorted to the ultimate strategy for political survival: engineering a crisis of faith

Monks were no longer merely seekers of internal purification or community educators; they were transformed into the structural guardians of a majoritarian, unitary state polity. By establishing this framework, post-colonial political actors on both sides of the aisle created a monster. They invited the monkhood into the arena of partisan politics, setting a dangerous precedent where the robe could be traded for policy leverage, state patronage, and eventually, immunity from the law.

Two Buddhisms

We seem to practice two kinds of Buddhism: the sublime compassion of Prince Siddhartha, and the capricious priestly vocation evident in the ongoing protest at the public park. This structural division brings us directly to the profound observations of another towering scholar, S.J. Tambiah.

In his classic and controversial text Buddhism Betrayed?, Tambiah wrote extensively about what can be conceptualised as ‘Two Buddhisms’ coexisting within the Sri Lankan consciousness.

The first is the Buddhism of the texts—a path of sublime compassion. This is the ethically elevated philosophy that preaches universal loving-kindness (Metta), psychological liberation, inner peace, and the transcendence of worldly attachments. This is the Buddhism that inspired the moral imagination of millions and produced centuries of artistic and philosophical genius.

The second, however, is a Buddhism driven by a capricious priestly vocation. This version represents the dark underside of the institution: a caste-entrenched, politically hyperactive monastic hierarchy that manipulates religious sentiment for temporal security.

When Buddhism is reduced from a path of spiritual awakening to a protective guild for the clerical class, it sheds its ethical imperatives. Tambiah warned that when this capricious, defensive majoritarian complex takes over, the Sasana becomes an instrument of exclusion, division, and aggression. The ‘Saffron Circus’ at Viharamahadevi Park is the ultimate manifestation of this dark underside, where spiritual duties are abandoned in favour of political grandstanding.

Yesterday’s politics fighting the future

The strange alignment of varied actors at Viharamahadevi Park makes complete sense when viewed through the lens of recent electoral shifts, particularly the National People’s Power (NPP) gaining a two-thirds majority under President Anura Kumara Dissanayake. Following these seismic democratic shifts and subsequent anti-corruption crackdowns, the old political guard has found itself utterly displaced. The political architecture of patronage, nepotism, and systemic corruption that governed Sri Lanka for decades has been soundly rejected by an electorate demanding fundamental structural change.

If Sri Lanka is to emerge from this chronic crisis of faith and governance, we—the Buddhist laity—must learn to decouple the sublime ethical framework of the historical Buddha from the self-serving acrobatics of the ‘Saffron Circus.’ . It is time to reject the apostates who desecrate the robe for political theatre and demand a return to a Buddhism defined not by majoritarian supremacy and occult curses, but by wisdom, intellectual rigour, and absolute compassion

Faced with this stark structural irrelevance and impending legal accountability for past follies, defeated opposition groups have resorted to the ultimate strategy for political survival: engineering a crisis of faith. Deprived of a credible economic program or a visionary governance alternative, the fractured opposition has hitched its wagon to the oldest, most reliable populist anchor available. They are exploiting the inherent anxieties of traditionalists by manufacturing a false narrative that the current state apparatus is bent on destroying the Sasana.

This voodoo stratagem has the hallmarks of the marketing wizards behind the Sarva Jana Balaya, and it seems to have seduced elements of the Samagi Jana Balawegaya (SJB) as well. The strategy is transparent: hide behind the sacred robe to secure personal protection, evade judicial scrutiny, and derail progressive legislative or anti-corruption efforts. It is transactional politics at its absolute worst. Politicians provide funds, logistical support, and media amplification; in return, rogue monastics provide a religious human shield, transforming what should be a criminal or political accountability process into a false defence of the faith.

Robed charlatans weaponising piety

What makes this mobilisation particularly insidious is the collusion between discredited political forces and robed charlatans who weaponise the blind piety of ordinary lay devotees. Laymen, confusing the defence of an ordained hierarchy with the defence of the Buddha›s actual teachings, are cynically manipulated into joining these pseudo-religious agitations.

This institutional complicity should not be ignored. The silent or unconcealed support offered by influential chapters, such as the Kotte Samagri Sangha Sabha, provides these fringe elements with a veneer of institutional legitimacy. When established Nikayas fail to discipline monastics who openly engage in political subversion and heresy, they degrade their own spiritual authority, reducing the Sangha to a mere factional interest group.

Nowhere is this decay more vividly captured than in the figure of Samantha Bhadra (formerly Pitiduwe Siridhamma). Emerging originally as a charismatic preacher who claimed advanced spiritual realisations, his trajectory has devolved into a grotesque caricature of monasticism. His organisation of the Mahason Pideniya in a public park under the guise of political protest is an act of absolute spiritual apostasy.

Mahasona is a demon of the graveyard—a symbol of fear, destruction, and delusion. It is an explicit admission that this brand of political Buddhism has completely emptied itself of the Dhamma, replacing the quest for Nirvana with the invocation of dark forces to curse political adversaries.

Black Magic in Park

The tragedy of the Viharamahadevi Park spectacle is that it exploits a deeply held cultural identity to serve the narrow interests of an elite political class and its monastic allies.

When Buddhism is reduced to public black magic, political sit-ins, and the defence of individuals accused of secular crimes, it loses its universal moral authority.

If Sri Lanka is to emerge from this chronic crisis of faith and governance, we—the Buddhist laity—must learn to decouple the sublime ethical framework of the historical Buddha from the self-serving acrobatics of the ‘Saffron Circus.’

We must look back to the warnings of Seneviratne and Tambiah to recognise that the politicisation of religion has brought nothing but moral and social bankruptcy. It is time to reject the apostates who desecrate the robe for political theatre and demand a return to a Buddhism defined not by majoritarian supremacy and occult curses, but by wisdom, intellectual rigour, and absolute compassion.
