title: Democracy, monkhood and economy | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 24 October 2026 00:00
-     - 9

Buddhist clergy surround the Presidential Secretariat demanding the release of Ven. Galagoda Aththe Gnanasara Thera

- Pic by Shehan Gunasekara

“Democracy has to be born anew every generation, and education is its midwife.”

- John Dewey

Introduction: National controversy with economic consequences

Sri Lanka’s current controversy surrounding sections of the Buddhist clergy, the imprisonment of Ven. Galagoda Aththe Gnanasara Thera, and demands for his release raises questions that extend far beyond an individual monk. At its heart lies a fundamental issue: How should a democratic society reconcile religious respect, monastic discipline, rule of law and authority of an elected Government?

The controversy is not simply about a robe, a prison sentence or a demonstration. It concerns the relationship between individual conduct and institutional responsibility, between religious influence and democratic accountability, and between political confrontation and national development.

The ultimate test of both democracy and monkhood is not the power to command others, but the wisdom to exercise one’s own responsibilities properly. Sri Lanka must protect the Dhamma without placing anyone above the law, strengthen democracy without silencing religious counsel, and pursue economic recovery without wasting the nation’s limited resources on avoidable confrontation. That is not a choice between Buddhism, democracy and development. It is a common path towards a more just, responsible and prosperous Sri Lanka

Sri Lanka cannot afford to treat these questions as isolated religious or political disputes. Following a period of severe economic instability, the country needs public institutions that inspire confidence, policies that encourage productive investment, and a society willing to direct its limited resources towards improving the lives of its people.

My argument is straightforward: democracy must be practised as a way of life, monkhood must be understood as an ethical discipline, and economic recovery must be protected from avoidable political and institutional disruption.

These objectives are not contradictory. Properly understood, they reinforce one another.

Democracy is more than the right to vote

Democracy is commonly understood as a system in which citizens elect their representatives. Elections are indispensable, but they are not the entirety of democracy.

A genuinely democratic society also requires respect for the law, freedom of expression, equality before the law, institutional independence, peaceful disagreement and mutual respect. These principles must govern relationships between citizens, between citizens and the State, and between institutions exercising different forms of authority.

Democracy therefore has a social and cultural dimension. It requires people to recognise that disagreement does not justify intimidation, that influence does not confer unlimited power, and that no individual or institution possesses an automatic entitlement to dictate outcomes to others.

Sri Lanka’s elected Government has a responsibility to govern within the Constitution and the law. Religious leaders have every right to advise, criticise and seek changes in Government policy. Citizens, including Buddhist monks, also possess rights of peaceful expression and assembly, subject to lawful restrictions.

However, the right to express an opinion is not the same as the authority to compel the Government to accept it. Nor does an electoral mandate entitle the Government to disregard the rights of those who disagree with it.

Democracy requires both sides to recognise these boundaries.

The question is not whether monks should participate in public debate. They should be free to do so. The question is whether participation should take the form of reasoned persuasion and lawful engagement or become an attempt to exercise coercive authority over democratic institutions.

Monkhood begins in the mind, not in the robe

A Buddhist monk is known in Pali as a bhikkhu and in Sanskrit as a bhikshu. The word bhikkhu is traditionally associated with one who lives by alms and, within Buddhist teaching, with the pursuit of liberation from suffering and the cycle of birth and death.

Ordination is not merely a change of clothing or social status. It represents a commitment to a disciplined way of life grounded in ethical conduct, restraint, wisdom and the pursuit of spiritual understanding.

This leads to an important distinction.

The robe is a visible symbol of monkhood, but the ethical substance of monkhood must be reflected in the mind and conduct of the person wearing it. One must cultivate the capacity to distinguish what is right from what is wrong, what is relevant from what is irrelevant, and what serves the public good from what serves personal ambition.

In this article, I use the idea of mindhood to describe this internal ethical discipline: the ability to examine one’s own intentions, exercise restraint and act with wisdom rather than anger, ego or the desire for power.

This is not a substitute for the established Buddhist concept of monkhood. It is an argument that genuine monkhood requires an inner disposition consistent with its outward commitments.

The same principle applies to democracy. A person may possess the formal right to vote while failing to respect democratic values in everyday life. Similarly, a person may wear the robe while acting in ways inconsistent with the discipline the robe represents.

The issue is therefore not the appearance of a monk but the relationship between religious status and ethical responsibility.

A robe deserves respect because of the spiritual tradition it represents; it cannot, by itself, establish the moral correctness of every action taken by its wearer.

The Buddha’s Teaching and the Responsibilities of Power

Buddhist history recognises a role for monks in guiding rulers and contributing to public welfare. Monks can offer moral counsel, draw attention to injustice, encourage compassion and remind political leaders of their responsibilities towards society.

Such engagement can be valuable to democratic governance.

A ruler who listens to ethical criticism may make better decisions. A monk who challenges corruption, protects vulnerable people and encourages peaceful solutions can make a significant contribution to national development.

However, the capacity to advise does not automatically confer the authority to command.

The relationship between religious counsel and political power must preserve the responsibilities of both. Elected representatives are accountable for governing the country, while religious leaders are responsible for the integrity of their own conduct and the quality of the guidance they provide.

The Buddhist tradition offers a useful ethical framework through the emphasis on right speech, restraint, compassion and the avoidance of harm. These principles encourage dialogue rather than hostility and reflection rather than impulsive confrontation.

The Sinhala expression associated with Ven. Galkande Dhammananda Thera in the current debate captures the spirit of a civilized solution: “ශීලාචාර විදිහට උත්තර හොයන්න” — seek answers in a civilized manner.

This is not a call for silence. It is a call for a better method of resolving disagreement.

When a religious institution has concerns about prison regulations, the treatment of an ordained person or the relationship between civil law and monastic discipline, those concerns should be examined through evidence, legal reasoning, dialogue and appropriate institutional procedures.

Respect for Buddhism does not require abandoning these processes. Indeed, the credibility of Buddhism is strengthened when its representatives demonstrate the discipline, restraint and wisdom that its teachings encourage.

Rule of law must protect everyone equally

The present controversy illustrates why a clear distinction must be maintained between a criminal sentence and the religious status of the person serving it.

The legal proceedings concerning Gnanasara Thera have included the invalidation of a previous presidential pardon and the enforcement of the remaining prison sentence for contempt of court. The separate dispute over prison attire has generated objections from sections of the Buddhist clergy. These are related public controversies, but they are not identical legal questions.

The State must act within the law, and prison authorities must follow applicable regulations. Equally, questions about the proper treatment of an ordained monk should be considered carefully, with due regard to lawful prison procedures and the relevant religious disciplinary framework.

The answer is neither automatic deference to religious authority nor unnecessary confrontation with it. It is a transparent, lawful and consistent process.

A democratic Government should not grant preferential treatment merely because a convicted person holds religious office. Nor should a person’s religious identity become a reason for humiliating or unfairly treating that person.

The principle is equal treatment under the law, accompanied by respect for legitimate religious freedom.

If there is a legal ambiguity concerning prison attire or the respective responsibilities of State authorities and monastic institutions, it should be clarified through proper legal and administrative channels. If changes are required, they should be made transparently and applied consistently, not introduced as a concession to political pressure.

The same principle applies to the Government. An elected administration must be prepared to explain its decisions and accept lawful scrutiny.

The rule of law is not an instrument for humiliating religion. It is a common safeguard against the arbitrary exercise of power by anyone, regardless of position, political affiliation or religious standing.

When religious and political confrontation weakens governance

Public demonstrations are a legitimate feature of democracy. They allow citizens to express grievances, challenge decisions and demand accountability. Their legitimacy, however, does not make every demand justified or every method appropriate.

The recent protests in Colombo over Gnanasara Thera’s release demonstrate how a dispute involving religious identity and State authority can absorb the attention of political leaders, public officials and the wider community. Reporting on the demonstrations also records court intervention concerning the protesters’ continued presence near the Presidential Secretariat, followed by discussions with the Ministry of Buddhasasana.

The lesson is not that religious leaders should avoid public affairs. It is that disputes must be resolved through institutions capable of examining the issues impartially.

When political actors mobilise religious sentiment to pressure the Government, the judiciary or public officials, they risk converting a question of law and procedure into a contest of political strength.

Such conduct can weaken institutional confidence. It may also encourage future groups to believe that sufficient public pressure can secure exceptions unavailable to other citizens.

This creates a dangerous precedent.

Today, the dispute may concern a monk. Tomorrow, it may concern a politician, businessperson, public official or another influential individual. If institutional decisions become negotiable according to the strength of a constituency rather than the merits of a case, equal citizenship is undermined.

The Government must therefore distinguish between listening to religious concerns and surrendering its constitutional responsibilities. Dialogue is a strength; capitulation to coercion is not.

Religious institutions, in turn, should recognise that their long-term credibility depends not on their capacity to mobilise crowds but on the quality of their ethical leadership.

Economic cost of distraction

Sri Lanka’s economic recovery requires more than improved macroeconomic indicators. Stabilisation must become a platform for investment, production, exports, employment and better living standards.

Every public resource has an alternative use. Money spent on organising and sustaining prolonged confrontations cannot simultaneously be used for education, healthcare, skills development, community services or productive investment. Public officials’ time is also scarce. Time spent managing avoidable institutional disputes is time unavailable for implementing economic policy and improving public services.

This does not mean that demonstrations are inherently wasteful. Peaceful protest can expose injustice, improve accountability and lead to better policy. The relevant question is whether the objective is legitimate, whether the method is proportionate, and whether the dispute is being pursued through appropriate channels.

Sri Lanka needs a more disciplined approach to the use of public and private resources.

Investors consider the predictability of laws, the reliability of public institutions and the possibility of political disruption when making investment decisions. Businesses need confidence that contracts will be respected, disputes will be resolved fairly and public policy will not be arbitrarily altered under pressure from powerful interest groups.

Persistent institutional confrontation can weaken that confidence. It can divert attention from reforms, complicate policy implementation and reinforce perceptions that influence matters more than rules.

The economic chain is clear: institutional credibility supports investment; investment supports production; production and competitiveness strengthen exports; exports generate foreign exchange; and stronger productive capacity improves the country’s ability to service debt and raise living standards.

Sri Lanka cannot afford to interrupt this process unnecessarily.

The Government must focus on expanding productive capacity, improving the business environment, encouraging export-oriented investment, strengthening public administration and ensuring that the benefits of recovery reach the wider community.

Religious leaders and political organisations can contribute by promoting social stability, ethical conduct and cooperation. They should not allow avoidable confrontations to displace the country’s economic priorities.

From political theatre to national development

Sri Lanka needs a constructive relationship between religious institutions, elected Government and civil society. Such a relationship should not be built on subordination or confrontation, but on clearly understood responsibilities.

The Government should engage respectfully with the Maha Sangha and other religious communities when legitimate concerns arise. It should explain the legal basis of its decisions, provide channels for consultation and ensure that public officials act professionally and consistently.

The judiciary must remain independent. The police and prison authorities must implement lawful decisions without political favouritism. Religious authorities should address questions of monastic discipline through their own appropriate procedures, while respecting the country’s legal framework.

Political parties, meanwhile, should resist the temptation to exploit religious sentiment for short-term advantage.

These responsibilities can be translated into a practical program:

These measures would help move the country away from recurring confrontations and towards a culture of institutional responsibility.

Democracy, monkhood and mindhood: A common ethical foundation

Democracy and monkhood may appear to belong to different spheres of life. Democracy concerns the organisation of public power, while monkhood concerns a religious vocation. Yet both depend, in important respects, on ethical conduct.

Democracy requires citizens and institutions to recognise limits on their own power. Monkhood requires an individual to cultivate restraint, wisdom and an understanding of the responsibilities associated with renunciation.

The concept of mindhood brings these ideas together by emphasising the internal discipline needed to act responsibly.

A democratic politician must understand that an electoral mandate is a responsibility, not a personal entitlement. A public official must understand that authority exists to serve the public, not to protect personal interests. A Buddhist monk must understand that spiritual influence is most valuable when exercised through ethical example, reasoned counsel and compassion.

These are different roles, but each requires a willingness to distinguish personal ambition from the common good.

This is also why the argument must not be reduced to a conflict between the Government and the Sangha. Such a framing would be both unnecessarily divisive and intellectually inadequate. Sri Lanka needs the constructive contribution of Buddhist monks and all other religious communities. It also needs the confidence that public institutions will operate according to law rather than pressure.

The objective is not to diminish religion’s place in society. It is to protect the integrity of religion and democracy alike.

Conclusion: Protect the Dhamma, strengthen democracy, rebuild the economy

Sri Lanka stands to gain little from turning the present controversy into a prolonged contest between the Government and sections of the Buddhist clergy. Nor would it benefit from treating every concern raised by a monk as illegitimate.

The civilized solution is to distinguish legitimate religious concerns from demands for exceptional treatment, and lawful public criticism from attempts to compel democratic institutions.

Monks must remain free to advise rulers, criticise injustice and contribute to the welfare of society. Elected governments must remain responsible for governing under the Constitution and the law. Courts must be able to discharge their duties independently. Religious institutions must be able to preserve monastic discipline without being used as instruments of political power.

Above all, the robe should not become a substitute for ethical conduct, just as an electoral mandate should not become a substitute for good governance.

Sri Lanka’s economic future depends on public trust, institutional credibility, productive investment and the responsible use of scarce resources. These cannot flourish indefinitely in an environment where every disagreement becomes a confrontation and every institution seeks to establish the supremacy of its own authority.

The country needs fewer contests over status and more commitment to public service; fewer attempts to compel and more willingness to persuade; less political theatre and greater economic productivity.

The Buddha’s teaching should not be invoked selectively to defend institutional privilege. It should encourage reflection, restraint, compassion and a civilized search for solutions. Democracy, likewise, must be more than a procedure for electing rulers. It must be a shared commitment to living together under fair rules.

The ultimate test of both democracy and monkhood is not the power to command others, but the wisdom to exercise one’s own responsibilities properly.

Sri Lanka must protect the Dhamma without placing anyone above the law, strengthen democracy without silencing religious counsel, and pursue economic recovery without wasting the nation’s limited resources on avoidable confrontation.

That is not a choice between Buddhism, democracy and development. It is a common path towards a more just, responsible and prosperous Sri Lanka.

(The author served as the Special Adviser to the Office of the President of Namibia from 2006 to 2012 and was a senior consultant with the UNDP for 20 years, and a Senior Economist with the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (1972-1992). He can be reached at asoka.seneviratne@gmail.com)

title: Proposed laws risk entrenching State power and enabling repression | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 24 October 2026 00:00
-     - 11

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake

These draft laws raise fundamental questions about the direction of governance reform in Sri Lanka. They concentrate powers that could be abused if not now in the future. Sri Lanka needs effective institutions capable of confronting corruption, organised crime and threats to public safety

By The National Peace Council 

The NPP Government’s determination to tackle corruption, drug trafficking and organised crime, including criminality involving powerful politicians and senior state officials, presents a significant break with the past. Its mandate for system change requires both effective law enforcement and protection against arbitrary state power.  

In this light,  the National Peace Council (NPC) is deeply concerned that three bills now before Parliament pull in the opposite direction. These are the Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill, the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill and the NGO Registration and Supervision Bill. Their provisions raise serious concerns about excessive state power and the potential for repression, now or under future Governments.

The Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill risks bringing legitimate political protest, trade union action and civil disobedience within the scope of terrorism offences. It provides for prolonged detention, inadequate judicial oversight and restrictions on access to legal counsel. 

Sri Lanka’s experience with the Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA) shows how such provisions are used against critics, minorities and political opponents. Any replacement must break decisively with this history and ensure meaningful judicial oversight, prompt access to legal counsel and effective remedies against arbitrary detention. Several petitions challenging the Bill were taken up before the Supreme Court. NPC trusts the outcome will ensure the proper balance that protects human rights and democratic freedoms.

The Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill has come before Parliament without public discussion. It provides for extensive surveillance powers, detention of up to a year and the admissibility of confessions made to the police. Ironically, provisions from the PTA, which is to be repealed, have come back through the backdoor in this draft law. The fight against organised crime is essential, but it must not create a separate criminal justice regime in which ordinary safeguards are diminished. Admitting confessions made in police custody invites coercion, as the record of PTA abuse shows. 

The proposed NGO legislation would give the state broad discretionary powers over the registration, renewal, suspension and deregistration of civil society organisations, including NPC, placing them under excessive administrative control. This threatens freedom of association, expression and independent advocacy, on which a democracy depends. Civil society plays an essential role in strengthening accountability, supporting vulnerable communities and promoting reconciliation. Its independence must be protected, not undermined by disproportionate regulatory control.

Taken together, these draft laws raise fundamental questions about the direction of governance reform in Sri Lanka. They concentrate powers that could be abused if not now in the future. Sri Lanka needs effective institutions capable of confronting corruption, organised crime and threats to public safety. It also needs institutions that protect citizens from abuses of state power. These objectives are complementary, not contradictory. It is essential for the Government to substantially revise the three bills where their provisions fail to meet constitutional and international human rights standards.

title: The Gnanasara Thera pardon | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 24 October 2026 00:00
-     - 9

Ven. Galagoda Aththe Gnanasara Thera in prison dress

Of all contempts committed against the lawful authority of courts of law the most heinous are those which involve actual or threatened injury to the person of a judge with a view to intimidating him into revoking or altering an order or decision made by him in the discharge of his judicial duties. The outrageous nature of the acts committed by the respondent constitutes not only an affront to the dignity and authority of the court but also a direct challenge to the fundamental supremacy of the law itself. It is a type of contemptuous conduct which appeared to us to be unprecedented in the annals of the courts of this country. Viewed in this light the circumstances of this case call for very deterrent punishment on the respondent

In a judgment delivered recently, a three-judge bench of the Supreme Court headed by Justice Janak de Silva, declared that the pardon granted to Ven. Galagoda Aththe Gnanasera Thera on 25 March 2019 by former President Maithripala Sirisena was null and void and was of no force or effect in law. The jurisdiction of the Court had been invoked in two fundamental rights applications filed by Dr. Paikiasothy Saravanamuttu and Sandhya Ekneligoda.  The former President was reported to have apologised to the Maha Sangha for “a technical error in the documentation” relating to the presidential pardon he purported to grant.  That technical error, he claimed, was “the failure to obtain the required approval from the Justice Ministry”.  He explained that “as a result, only my signature was obtained without the approval of the Justice Ministry. That was a failure on my part”.  He asserted that the Supreme Court had quashed the presidential pardon and committed the priest back into prison owing to that omission.  President Sirisena has, either deliberately, inadvertently, or in ignorance, totally misinterpreted the judgment of the Supreme Court.

The constitutional requirement to seek the advice of the Justice Minister, and examine reports from the trial judge and the Attorney-General, arises only in the case of a prisoner who had been sentenced to death by a competent court.  It is on a consideration of those documents that the President is required to determine whether to let the law take its course or to commute the sentence of death to one of life imprisonment.  That procedural requirement did not exist in the case of Gnanasara Thero.  Therefore, President Sirisena’s excuse of a “technical error” has no basis in law or fact.

Magistrate’s Court of Homagama

On 26 January 2016, the suspects in the case relating to the disappearance of journalist Prageeth Ekneligoda were produced in the Magistrate’s Court of Homagama.  During the proceedings, Gnanasara Thero, who was not a party to the proceedings or a witness, had entered the courtroom and (i) obstructed the proceedings by beginning to address the Magistrate; (ii) declared that he would not accept the orders of the Magistrate; (iii) ordered the Magistrate to grant bail to the suspects; and (iv) described the Senior State Counsel who was appearing for the prosecution as “an impotent state officer”.  This violent display of verbal threats or open defiance directed at the Magistrate constituted contempt of court.  

Court of Appeal

In March 2016, in proceedings instituted in the Court of Appeal under Article 105 of the Constitution, upon a reference by the Magistrate, Gnanasara Thero was convicted on all four counts of contempt. He was sentenced to serve four years of imprisonment in respect of (i) and (ii); six years in respect of (iii), and five years in respect of (iv), the sentences to run concurrently.

The pardon

On 23 May 2019, President Sirisena granted a pardon to Gnanasara Thera, who was thereupon released from prison.  Shortly thereafter, the Centre for Policy Alternatives and Dr. Paikiasothy Saravanamuttu, and Mrs. Sandhya Ekneligoda, filed applications in the Supreme Court under Articles 17 and 126, asserting the grant of pardon to be an infringement of their fundamental right to equality and the equal protection of the law.  It was six years later, in August 2005 that the two applications were listed for hearing before a Bench of the Supreme Court comprising Justices Janak de Silva, Sobhitha Rajakaruna and Sampath Abayakoon.

Supreme Court

 According to the documentary trail placed before the Supreme Court, it appeared that a pardon had been requested by the Mahanayake Theros of the Malwatte, Asgiriya and Kotte Chapters of the Siyam Nikaya, as well as by the Diyawadana Nilame. There was also a letter bearing several names requesting President Sirisena not to grant a pardon. While President Sirisena had been made aware of these requests from time to time, the pardon was eventually granted by him on the basis of a minute submitted to him by the Additional Secretary (Legal) in the Presidential Secretariat, Lakshmi Jayawickrema.  

That minute did not disclose any reason why the President should consider granting a pardon. Nevertheless, he approved the granting of a pardon. No reasons for the grant of the pardon were recorded by the President. As the Supreme Court noted, “it is apparent that the President, by simply approving the recommendation of the Additional Secretary (Legal), acted mechanically and abdicated the exercise of the power and responsibilities vested in him”. Accordingly, the Court held that the pardon granted to Gnanasara Thero was “arbitrary, in violation of the public trust and the rules of natural justice, ultra vires the powers of the President, and was an infringement of the fundamental rights guaranteed by Article 12(1) of the Constitution. It had no force or effect in law.

In his judgment, Justice Janak de Silva noted that under the Constitution, 

“The President exercises the executive power of the People. As the repository of that executive power, the President holds such power in trust for and on behalf of the People. It follows that the exercise of such power must be directed towards the public interest and cannot be permitted to be exercised for any personal, political or other self-serving interest. . . A pardon is not a private act of grace exercised for the benefit of the President . . . It is an exercise of a constitutional power derived from the sovereignty of the People and must, therefore, be directed to an end which is consistent with the public interest.”  

The Court held that the President is under a duty to make a contemporaneous record of the reasons for the grant of a pardon, and to make such reasons available to any aggrieved party when requested, and to the Court when the decision is impugned. In this case, the former President had failed to state in his affidavit the reasons for the grant of the pardon. He had merely stated that the grant of pardon was preceded by requests from several distinguished members of the Buddhist clergy and other religious denominations, and by representatives of civil society. 

Justice Janak de Silva cited with approval the following observations made by the late Justice Atukorale to explain the nature of the offence of contempt committed in a Magistrate’s Court:

“A Magistrate’s Court is one of the institutions created and established for the administration of justice in this country. For this purpose, a Magistrate is entrusted with the performance of important judicial functions and duties. In the course of the performance of such functions and duties he is called upon to make various decisions and orders. There is no decision or order he can make which cannot be challenged. But the challenge must be by an appropriate application or proceeding made to this court in accordance with law. It cannot be challenged by a violent display of verbal threats or open defiance directed at the Magistrate himself. 

Of all contempts committed against the lawful authority of courts of law the most heinous are those which involve actual or threatened injury to the person of a judge with a view to intimidating him into revoking or altering an order or decision made by him in the discharge of his judicial duties. The outrageous nature of the acts committed by the respondent constitutes not only an affront to the dignity and authority of the court but also a direct challenge to the fundamental supremacy of the law itself. It is a type of contemptuous conduct which appeared to us to be unprecedented in the annals of the courts of this country. . . .Viewed in this light the circumstances of this case call for very deterrent punishment on the respondent.”

title: Beyond the robe: Sangha, rule of law and monastic accountability | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 24 October 2026 00:00
-     - 10

Avukana Buddha statue

In the context of a monastic institution, the answer cannot lie in assuming that religious status places an individual beyond ordinary legal obligations, or in automatically deferring to every decision made by the State

I have been aghast at the drama that unfolded over the last several days, both in and outside Parliament, in and outside Buddhist temples, on and off the streets, and in and outside parks - otherwise reserved for the less  privileged public who have neither large homes and gardens, nor temples or V8 vehicles to exercise or take shelter in.

I was taken aback by the positions taken by representatives of political parties, now in the collective opposition, some sitting in as peoples representatives and others acting outside Parliament, several of who I know and have known, worked and interacted with for decades. The tone and substance of certain statements, letters, articles, speeches, video footage and the publicly aired opinions of some, were I thought, inconsistent and in conflict with the positions they took, or the stance they had adopted years before. Were they politically biased and even intellectually dishonest, I wondered. Representatives of the monkhood in robes, were sadly, disgracefully disruptive, dangerously provocative and inciteful, grossly disrespectful, and in conflict with the teachings of the Buddha whose Dhamma they had chosen to help people learn from, understand, identify with and practice.

Of monks and men

All this of monks and men, women too, can undoubtedly be dangerous, and a shockingly bad example to a wide cross section of society. Over and above all this, the message we have sent to the outside world - of a disruptive society rather than one which is a destination for tourism, foreign direct and portfolio investment and a home to live in, return to and bring up children in - is clearly shortsighted and irresponsible.

The ‘beyond’ series

As I thought deeply about all of the above and wondered why, a Sri Lankan - a fellow Chartered Accountant, who I have known for decades and who considered returning in 2009, after our "war" was over, called me last week from overseas where he chose to remain. In late 2009, 16 years ago, he had told me that he considered returning, having also been encouraged by my articles titled "Beyond the Day to Day Military Conflict"; "Beyond Bullets and Bayonets"  "Beyond the IMF Bailout" ( we had bailouts many decades ago too)," "Transitioning from Brain Drain to Brain Gain"  (of this he said I was hinting at him, because the version in a Sunday paper had a cartoon with a brain carrying a briefcase and returning home to Sri-Lanka ). There were also my articles titled "Towards National Reconciliation - Towards interreligious, interracial, inter communal harmony" and the more recent "Beyond Judicial Tenure". Referring to all this and more, he asked me why I had not written an article on "Beyond the Robe." I actually had written exactly that, but not edited it for release due to competing demands on my time. So here it is now!

Beyond an individual controversy

The controversy surrounding the wearing of robes by Ven. Galagoda Aththe Gnanasara Thero while serving a prison sentence raises questions extending well beyond one individual or one prison decision. It invites a broader examination of the relationship between the State, the Buddhist Sangha, the Constitution, the administration of justice and the institutions responsible for upholding standards of conduct.

This article is not an argument for or against a presidential pardon, or about eligibility or otherwise for a robe in court or outside in prison or otherwise of one individual. Nor does it seek to revisit a judicial determination through public commentary, prejudge the ethics, the morality, administrative appropriateness or legality of a prison decision or an attempt to determine the Thero's monastic status. Those questions must be addressed by the institutions competent to decide them.

Convicted prisoners and Buddhist monks

The wider issues nevertheless deserve careful consideration. How should the State exercise its authority over a convicted prisoner who is also an ordained Buddhist monk? Who should determine whether a monk has breached the Vinaya or ceased to qualify for monastic status? How can the autonomy of the Sangha be respected while ensuring that public institutions act lawfully and that religious institutions maintain credible standards of discipline and accountability? These are not necessarily competing concerns. A mature constitutional democracy must find ways to uphold them together.

The Robe - A symbol of renunciation, discipline, commitment, not immunity

I am a practising Buddhist. I am in close touch with and have a mutually respectful relationship with three temples in my village of birth and two in the city of Colombo. I subscribe to the Buddhist philosophy, but not necessarily to all of the rituals of many.  But for all of us Buddhists, the robe is far more than an item of clothing. It represents renunciation, discipline and commitment to a religious way of life. Its significance extends beyond the individual monk to the Sangha and the Buddha Sasana. That significance warrants sensitivity in the administration of prisons. But sensitivity is not the same as immunity from the law. Equally, imprisonment does not automatically settle every question concerning a prisoner's religious or ecclesiastical status.

Criminal liability, ecclesiastical authority and monastic discipline

Three matters must be distinguished. A criminal court determines criminal liability and imposes a sentence. The State administers that sentence under the applicable law. The relevant ecclesiastical authority addresses questions of monastic discipline and status within its proper jurisdiction. A criminal conviction does not, by itself, establish every consequence that may follow under the Vinaya. Conversely, continued recognition as a monk does not invalidate a conviction or remove the obligation to comply with a lawful sentence. The question is therefore not whether a monk should be exempt from the law. It is whether the State's treatment of a monk in custody is authorised by law, consistent with applicable prison rules and implemented fairly.

The constitutional balance: Religious protection and the rule of law

Sri Lanka's Constitution provides an important framework for considering these questions. Its provisions must be read together rather than selectively invoking one article while overlooking others.

Article 9 gives Buddhism the foremost place and places an obligation on the State to protect and foster the Buddha Sasana, while assuring the rights guaranteed to other religions under Articles 10 and 14(1)(e). Article 10 protects freedom of thought, conscience and religion, while Article 14(1)(e) recognises the freedom to manifest religious belief or practice, subject to applicable constitutional limitations.

The State must act lawfully. Courts must be respected. The Sangha's legitimate religious authority must be recognised. Questions of monastic status must be addressed through appropriate ecclesiastical processes. Public allegations must be assessed fairly, and institutional standards must be capable of sustaining public confidence. Respect for the Sangha and respect for the rule of law are not opposing causes. Properly understood, each can strengthen the other. Only then can both retain their relevance and sustainability

Article 12 establishes equality before the law and equal protection of the law. Article 13 provides safeguards concerning personal liberty, arrest, detention and punishment. Article 11 prohibits torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. Article 15(7) permits prescribed legal restrictions on specified fundamental rights for stated purposes, including public order, public health or morality, the rights and freedoms of others, and the just requirements of a democratic society. Its scope must be understood from its actual wording; it is not an unrestricted power to limit every constitutional right. These provisions establish principles relevant to the debate, but they do not, without further legal analysis, settle the particular question of prison attire. Nor does Article 9 automatically determine how a departmental order should be interpreted.

The constitutional balance is neither that religious identity displaces the law nor that religious identity becomes irrelevant whenever the State exercises its powers. The State must act within the law, respect applicable constitutional protections and be able to justify its decisions by reference to the governing legal framework. Public officials, politicians, lawyers and commentators all have a responsibility. The rule of law is strengthened not by the force with which a position is asserted, but by the evidence and reasoning that sustain it.

The Sangha's role and judicial precedent

Senior Buddhist prelates have reportedly maintained that the question of whether a monk should be disrobed or cease to be recognised as a member of the Order is a matter for the relevant ecclesiastical authority. They have also expressed concern about the removal of robes in the course of imprisonment. These views deserve serious consideration.

However, reported statements should not be treated as conclusive determinations of either the applicable prison law or the Thero's monastic status. Sri Lanka has a history of ecclesiastical processes for addressing internal monastic disputes and discipline. In Rev. Keselwatugoda Chandananda Thero v. Rev. Sirimalwatte Ananda Mahanayaka Thero and Others (1996 2 SLR 287), the Court of Appeal considered an ecclesiastical inquiry into alleged indiscipline and recognised the significance of disciplinary processes established within the relevant monastic institution.

The broader lesson is that questions of monastic discipline should be addressed through the appropriate ecclesiastical authority and applicable procedures. The precedent does not, however, establish the current rules of every Nikaya or demonstrate that any particular institution's procedures are either adequate or inadequate today. The authority, rules and procedures of the relevant Nikaya or Sangha body must be established from its own authoritative documents.

Fair inquiry, ethical conduct and public responsibility

Credible concerns arise when there are public allegations about a monk’s conduct, language or behaviour, supported by reliable evidence. The appropriate ecclesiastical authority should consider them through a process consistent with its governing rules. Such a process should provide notice of the allegations, a fair opportunity to respond, and impartial consideration of the evidence and reasoned findings. Consequences should follow from the applicable rules and the findings. This protects both the individual concerned and the institution. It avoids prejudgment without allowing serious allegations to be dismissed merely because they concern a religious figure.

Confrontational public pressure vs. responsible advocacy

Public pressure should not become a means of circumventing judicial proceedings, and confrontational conduct should not substitute for lawful procedure. If senior clergy believe that a judicial or administrative decision warrants reconsideration, formal representations to the competent authority provide a responsible avenue. Religious leaders and public officials alike remain entitled to express reasoned views. The distinction is between responsible advocacy and conduct that disregards due process or seeks to substitute pressure for lawful decision-making.

The Dhammapada's teachings-guarded speech, body and mind.

The Buddhist ethical tradition places importance on restraint in speech and conduct. The Dhammapada's teachings on guarding speech, body and mind offer a relevant ethical reflection. They should not, however, be presented as proof that any individual has committed a specific Vinaya offence. Such a determination belongs to the appropriate ecclesiastical process, applying the relevant standards and evidence. The dignity of the Sangha is best protected through integrity, compassion, restraint and credible self-discipline—not through an assumption that questions of conduct must never be raised.

Lessons from regulation of professions and independent oversight

Many institutions offer useful, though not identical, examples of how autonomy can be combined with accountability. Professional bodies in accounting and law maintain standards of conduct and disciplinary arrangements for their members. In Sri Lanka, the Sri Lanka Accounting and Auditing Standards Monitoring Board provides an example of a statutory oversight mechanism operating alongside the professional framework for accounting and auditing. The Central Bank of Sri Lanka's fitness-and-propriety framework for directors of licensed banks offers another example of institutional standards intended to protect confidence in regulated institutions. These are analogies, not templates to be transplanted mechanically. The Sangha is a religious community governed by its traditions and the Vinaya, not a professional association or a commercial enterprise. Its institutional arrangements must reflect that distinctive character.

Intimidation, interference,

forbearance and conflict of interest

Drawing on my recent writings on possible political interference and influence of private vested interest, which may lead to the risk of regulatory forbearance, I believe a related governance question merits consideration. Where the governing body of a Nikaya is asked by a governmental authority, such as prison authorities, to provide guidance on the attire of a monk belonging to that Nikaya, who is serving a prison term, what safeguards ensure the independence of its deliberations, freedom from intimidation or improper interference, and the appropriate management of any actual or potential conflicts of interest? These are legitimate questions of institutional governance. They do not imply that any particular deficiency or conflict exists; that must be established by evidence. Nevertheless, the clarity and independence of disciplinary arrangements are relevant to the integrity, credibility and public confidence that a religious institution rightly seeks to sustain. Institutional accountability, properly understood, need not diminish the authority of the Sangha. It can help sustain the moral credibility upon which that authority ultimately depends.

Respect, authority and

monastic accountability

The controversy over the robe ultimately raises a question larger than clothing. How can citizens of a country, representatives of a community, members of a professional association, employees of a company, and monks belonging to a monastic institution or Nikaya retain the respect of others and preserve their dignity while remaining accountable for their conduct and the exercise of their authority?

In the context of a monastic institution, the answer cannot lie in assuming that religious status places an individual beyond ordinary legal obligations, or in automatically deferring to every decision made by the State. Institutional reform cannot be achieved by conflating ecclesiastical discipline with criminal punishment, either.

The State must act lawfully. Courts must be respected. The Sangha's legitimate religious authority must be recognised. Questions of monastic status must be addressed through appropriate ecclesiastical processes. Public allegations must be assessed fairly, and institutional standards must be capable of sustaining public confidence. Respect for the Sangha and respect for the rule of law are not opposing causes. Properly understood, each can strengthen the other. Only then can both retain their relevance and sustainability.

By Hishan Welmilla

Nagoya, Japan – Sri Lanka enjoyed a memorable day at the 5th Asian Para Games 2026 in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, with distance runner Pradeep Somasiri and long jumper Janani Dhananjana capturing gold medals, while Nuwan Indika Gamage secured silver in the men’s T44 100m. However, the day also brought disappointment as several Sri Lankan athletes narrowly missed out on podium finishes.

Pradeep Somasiri led Sri Lanka’s medal-winning performances with a historic victory in the men’s T46 1500m, clocking 4:03.25 to claim gold and establish a new Games record. His outstanding performance further confirmed his position among Asia’s leading para-athletes in the event.

Somasiri’s latest triumph was particularly significant as he had also won gold in the same event at the 2023 Asian Para Games in Hangzhou, China, where he set a Games record of 4:05.14. His performance in Nagoya improved that previous mark by 1.89 seconds, demonstrating his continued progress at the highest level of Asian para-athletics.

He had also delivered an impressive performance at the 2025 World Para Athletics Championships in New Delhi, India, winning bronze in the men’s T46 1500m while setting a new Asian record in the event.

Sri Lanka’s second gold medal came through Janani Dhananjana, who triumphed in the women’s T47 long jump with an impressive leap of 5.52 metres. Her victory established a new Games record and added another significant achievement to her campaign in Nagoya.

The gold medal marked Dhananjana’s second medal at the 2026 Games, underlining her consistency and competitive ability on the continental stage. She had earlier narrowly missed a podium finish in the women’s T47 100m, making her gold-medal performance in the long jump an impressive comeback.

Nuwan Indika Gamage added a silver medal to Sri Lanka’s tally in the men’s T44 100m, recording a season’s best time of 11.58 seconds. Although he could not repeat his gold-medal achievement from Hangzhou, Indika’s performance highlighted his continued competitiveness at the Asian level.

At the 2023 Asian Para Games, Indika won gold in the same event with a Games-record time of 11.63 seconds. His latest performance in Nagoya was 0.05 seconds faster than his previous Games-winning time, reflecting his progress despite finishing with silver this time.

Meanwhile, Sri Lanka’s medal hopes in the men’s F44 javelin throw suffered a setback when Samitha Dulan finished fourth. The former world record holder and reigning Asian record holder managed a best throw of 64.10 metres but was unable to secure a place on the podium.

Dulan had been among Sri Lanka’s leading medal prospects, and his fourth-place finish was a disappointing outcome for the Sri Lankan camp. Despite his considerable achievements in the event, the competition in Nagoya proved challenging as he fell short of the medals.

Sri Lankan swimmers Galina Bandara and Naveed Rahim also finished fourth in their respective 100m S9 finals. Galina clocked 1:09.00 in the women’s event, while Naveed recorded 58.78 seconds in the men’s final. Both athletes produced commendable performances but narrowly missed out on a place among the medal winners.

Buddika Indrapala was the final Sri Lankan athlete to compete in the day’s events, contesting the men’s T42 final where he finished fourth. 

Despite the disappointment of several fourth-place finishes, the gold medals won by Somasiri and Dhananjana, together with Indika’s silver, provided significant highlights for Sri Lanka at the continental competition.

The performances also demonstrated the determination and competitive spirit of Sri Lanka’s para-athletes, many of whom continued to challenge the region’s leading competitors in their respective events at the 5th Asian Para Games in Japan.

title: Let’s not make this historic win just a one-off show but a turning point | Daily FT

Moments to Cherish: Sri Lanka celebrate a historic win

By Sa’adi Thawfeeq

In recent times Sri Lanka have been known to pull off a stunning win from nowhere but fail to carry on that momentum.

We don’t want a repeat of what happened in England last month when Sri Lanka beaten comprehensively in the first ODI, roared back in the second to turn tables on the home side and level the series, giving hopes of a comeback, but only to fall flat on their face in the third ODI and get thrashed by a massive 223 runs.

Sri Lanka’s historic run chase is something to treasure for other than South Africa and India no team has chased over 400 in an ODI and won. When England ran up a mammoth 429-4 no one in his right mind would have put their money on Sri Lanka to chase it down and win. So inconsistent has been their performances in ODI cricket that it has come to a point that fans have started losing interest in watching the matches.

But Thursday’s astonishing win will certainly rekindle the interest once again. Could this be the turning point for Sri Lanka in ODI cricket?

The win could be what the Sri Lankan team needed to inject some life to their sagging fortunes. They have been at the receiving end of so many defeats that an occasional win is like gold dust. What Sri Lanka needs to do now is not rest on their laurels of this famous victory but to use that as a launch pad to further their success with an eye on next year’s Cricket World Cup. 

Nothing satisfies a cricket fan more than winning a trophy. Now that they have made a start and a most memorable one at that, what Sri Lanka needs to do is try and win the Pakistan ODI Tri-Series.

That opening match against Pakistan which Sri Lanka should have won but threw away due to the lack of common sense batting, certainly had its effects. Some strong words may have been spoken at the team meetings no less by a person than the head coach Gary Kirsten whose reaction when Janith Liyanage and Dasun Shanaka threw away their wickets went viral simply implying what he thought about the shots they played. Liyanage in fact took the blame for the defeat when he appeared at the post match press conference. Whatever that took place certainly had its effects the way the Lankan batsmen buckled down to their job of chasing down the record score in the next match.

It was Shanaka’s 50-ball blitz 97 that swung the game Sri Lanka’s way and it was Liyanage who provided the finishing touch to the match with a 27-ball cameo knock of 61*. They had certainly compensated for the mistakes they made in the first game.

There have been questions asked about Shanaka’s selection, captaincy and performances, and criticism is part of professional sport. But we all know what he is capable of when he gets going. On Thursday, he reminded everyone of his ability to change a match in a matter of overs.

Avishka Fernando recalled to the ODI side was somewhat under the pump after failing miserably in the first match, but given a second chance he seized it with both hands and was most unfortunate to miss out on a century by three runs. He is finding his feet once again in ODI cricket and if he can continue with the form he displayed, it will surely strengthen the bench when Pathum Nissanka returns from injury.

Pavan Rathnayake has scored both his ODI hundreds in his short career batting at number 4. His first hundred was scored when he was promoted to number 4 against England at the R Premadasa Stadium in January this year, and his second, a career best 130 was the cornerstone on which Sri Lanka built their mountainous run chase. He has more or less solved Sri Lanka’s no. 4 batting problems.

While we applaud the magnificent run chase and victory, everything is not right in the Sri Lankan unit. There are quite a few grey areas that need to be addressed, especially the bowling and the balance of the team.

Sri Lanka simply don’t have the bowlers who can clock 140 plus and penetrative spinners who can win matches for them. Sri Lanka won against England purely on their batting. They didn’t get their balance right with the bowling. They went with only four specialist bowlers and the lack of a fifth allowed England easy runs. The three who made up for the fifth bowler Shanaka, Liyanage and Kamindu Mendis leaked 123 runs off their combined 10 overs.

If one were to roll back the years, the 1996 Cricket World Cup triumph was won by outstanding batting and brilliant fielding. But times have changed and so has the game with two balls being used at the start of play and one after the 34th over so that reverse swing comes into play quite significantly. That is why Sri Lanka needs a good bowling unit to exploit the conditions.

Sri Lankan cricket has faced difficult questions in recent times, and one victory will not solve every problem. For now, let’s savour the moment, but we should not get too carried away by the win. Performances like this can change the mood inside a dressing room, restore belief and give players the confidence to compete against anyone. The coaching staff, too, will have plenty of positives to take from this incredible team effort.

England must be wondering what more they could have done with the bat even after scoring 429. Their captain Harry Brook smashed the fastest ODI double century and they still ended up on the losing side.

People have often questioned the future of the format, especially against the razzle-dazzle of T20 cricket. But matches like this remind us that the 50-over game can still deliver extraordinary drama, unbelievable comebacks and moments that stay with us for years. Like West Indies head coach Darren Sammy commented on social media: “Wow… no score is safe,” when his team was at the receiving end against India last month after scoring 405. It can happen when a team has belief and batters are willing to take responsibility like Sri Lanka did on Thursday.
